ch10.anchor: he sang in the market of Yan
ch10.note: The opening of Wang Jingwei's most famous poem, written in 1910 in a Qing prison as he awaited death for a failed plot to assassinate the Manchu Prince Regent: 'With ardor I sang in the market of Yan; serene, I play the captive of Chu; one clean stroke of the blade, and I shall not have wasted my young head.' 'The market of Yan' recalls the assassin Jing Ke, who sang there before his mission. The bitter irony is that this fearless young would-be martyr became, thirty years on, the great collaborator with Japan.

Kagesa Sadaaki (影佐禎昭, 1893–1948), the Japanese army officer who headed the 'Ume' (Plum) special-service agency and was the chief architect of Wang Jingwei's defection and puppet government—one of the Japanese army's leading China hands and the puppet regime's principal handler.

ch10.anchor: the Intelligence Bureau of the Ministry of National Defense
ch10.note: The postwar military-intelligence agency of the Nationalist government on Taiwan (国防部情报局), institutional heir to the wartime Juntong (by way of the Bureau of Confidential Investigation). It compiled the authorized life and papers of Dai Li that Chen cites here.

ch10.anchor: delivered an address formally proclaiming China's resolve to resist
ch10.note: Chiang Kai-shek's celebrated Lushan Declaration of 17 July 1937, ten days after the Marco Polo Bridge clash, in which he warned that once 'the last extremity' (最后关头) was reached the whole nation must fight to the end. It is remembered as the speech that committed China to all-out war.
